problem:
WO-0010 closed the non-finite defect on the dt parameter of WaveScheduler.Tick and PlayerMotor.Tick. The identical defect -- a guard whose predicate is a bare ordering comparison, which NaN fails to trip because every comparison against NaN is false -- survives on five other parameters of those same two types, including one on the very same call the fix hardened. WO-0010's criteria are scoped entirely to dt and say nothing about any of these, so this is not a failure against WO-0010 and I am filing no challenge over it. But the studio is about to record the dt defect class as closed, and it is not: three instances were closed and five were left, four of them in the two files that were open on the implementer's screen.

The live one is PlayerMotor.Tick's second parameter. Assets/Core/Player/PlayerMotor.cs:46-55: `if (moveAxis > 1f) moveAxis = 1f; else if (moveAxis < -1f) moveAxis = -1f;` -- both comparisons are false for NaN, so a NaN axis passes through unclamped into `PositionX = Clamp(PositionX + (moveAxis * _moveSpeed * dt))`. Clamp at lines 86-94 tests `x < _minX` then `x > _maxX`, both false for NaN, so it returns NaN unchanged. PositionX becomes NaN and stays NaN forever, because NaN plus anything is NaN on every subsequent tick. The player leaves the tracked bounds permanently, with no exception, no flag and no test failing. That is verbatim the failure mode PRO-0005 described for dt = NaN in this same method, still reachable, through the other argument of the same call: Assets/Unity/PlayerController.cs:33 is `_motor.Tick(Time.deltaTime, Input.GetAxisRaw("Horizontal"))`, and WO-0010 hardened the first argument only. Note that +/-Infinity on moveAxis is handled correctly (Infinity > 1f is true, so it clamps); NaN alone gets through, which is exactly why the existing test ClampsAxisSoAKeyboardCannotOutrunAGamepad passes on an axis of 50f and proves nothing about this.

The other four are constructor guards, and they are absorbing rather than loud. WaveScheduler.cs:29 `if (interval <= 0f)` is false for NaN, so a NaN interval is accepted by a guard whose message reads 'Interval must be > 0 or the scheduler would spawn forever within one tick'; the resulting scheduler adds NaN to _timeUntilNextSpawn and, since `NaN <= 0f` is false, never spawns again for the rest of the run. WaveScheduler.cs:35 `if (firstSpawnDelay < 0f)` accepts NaN identically, poisoning _timeUntilNextSpawn from construction so the scheduler never spawns at all. WaveScheduler.cs:41 `if (halfWidth < 0f)` accepts NaN, producing NaN spawn X coordinates. PlayerMotor.cs:20 `if (moveSpeed < 0f)` accepts NaN, and PlayerMotor.cs:25 `if (maxX <= minX)` is false when either bound is NaN, so a motor can be constructed whose Clamp can never do anything.

These are not reachable from Time.deltaTime, so they are less severe than the Tick defects. They are reachable from configuration, from Studio/sim, and from any future caller computing a construction parameter, and they share the exact property that made PRO-0002 and PRO-0005 expensive: the failure is silent and absorbing, so the first observable symptom is a run that quietly stops working.
evidence: Assets/Core/Player/PlayerMotor.cs:46-55 -- `if (moveAxis > 1f) ... else if (moveAxis < -1f) ...`; both branches are false for NaN, so NaN reaches the position update unclamped.

Assets/Core/Player/PlayerMotor.cs:86-94 -- `if (x < _minX) return _minX; return x > _maxX ? _maxX : x;`; both comparisons are false for NaN, so Clamp(NaN) returns NaN. PositionX is then NaN permanently, since line 55 adds to the previous PositionX on every subsequent tick.
Assets/Unity/PlayerController.cs:33 -- `_motor.Tick(Time.deltaTime, Input.GetAxisRaw("Horizontal"))`. WO-0010 hardened argument one of this exact call and left argument two open.

Assets/Core/Spawning/WaveScheduler.cs:29-33 -- `if (interval <= 0f) throw ... "Interval must be > 0 or the scheduler would spawn forever within one tick."`; NaN <= 0f is false, so the message states a predicate the guard does not enforce -- the identical mismatch PRO-0002 documented and WO-0010 criterion 12 exists to prevent.
Assets/Core/Player/PlayerMotor.cs:20-28 -- `if (moveSpeed < 0f)` false for NaN; `if (maxX <= minX)` false when either is NaN.

Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/PlayerMotorTests.cs -- the only axis-extremes test is ClampsAxisSoAKeyboardCannotOutrunAGamepad (line 36), which uses 50f. No test in the file passes a non-finite moveAxis. Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/WaveSchedulerTests.cs RejectsNonPositiveInterval (line 174) covers 0f and -1f only; no test passes a non-finite constructor argument to either type.

Assets/Core/DtGuard.cs now exists and states the predicate once. Nothing in it is specific to dt: `!float.IsFinite(x) || x < 0f` is the same check every one of the guards above needs, and the helper it belongs beside already sits in the namespace root.
proposedWork:
One L3 work order to engineering, scoped to Assets/Core/Player/**, Assets/Core/Spawning/** and Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/**.

(1) PlayerMotor.Tick must reject a non-finite moveAxis rather than pass it through. Either throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(moveAxis), moveAxis, "moveAxis must be a finite number.") immediately after the dt guard, or treat NaN as zero input; I recommend throwing, to match the treatment dt now gets on the same call and to keep the Core contract uniform, but the choice belongs to the order's author because it is a behaviour decision, not a correctness one. Whichever is chosen, the +/-Infinity path must keep clamping to +/-1 as it does today, and all 9 original PlayerMotorTests assertions must pass unmodified.

(2) The five constructor guards must state and enforce the predicates their messages already claim: WaveScheduler's interval (finite and > 0), firstSpawnDelay (finite and >= 0), halfWidth (finite and >= 0), PlayerMotor's moveSpeed (finite and >= 0) and the minX/maxX bound relation (both finite and maxX > minX).

(3) Generalise Assets/Core/DtGuard.cs rather than copying its body a sixth time. It is already the right shape and the wrong name; renaming it to a finite-argument guard with RequireFiniteNonNegative(value, paramName) and RequireFinite(value, paramName), and having every guard above call it, is what stops instance nine. If the order's author would rather not rename a file WO-0010 has only just created, adding the second method to DtGuard as-is is acceptable and the rename can be a separate cosmetic follow-up.

Every new regression test must be demonstrated failing against the unmodified code and passing after, per WO-0010 criterion 17. The PlayerMotor NaN-axis test is the important one and it fails loudly today without any special harness: construct a motor, Tick(0.1f, float.NaN), and assert PositionX is finite and within [minX, maxX]. It returns NaN against the current code. No bounded-buffer technique is needed anywhere in this order, because none of these defects is a hang.
expectedBenefit: Stops WO-0010 being recorded as having closed the non-finite guard defect class when it closed three of eight instances. Closes a permanent player-position corruption that is reachable from the shipped Unity shell through the second argument of the very call WO-0010 hardened, and five silent-configuration failures whose first symptom is a scheduler that stops spawning with nothing reported. Most durably, it converts the guard from a dt-specific helper into the single place the studio states what a finite argument means, which is the only version of this fix that a ninth instance cannot be written around.
notes:
Two adjacent limits examined this round and deliberately NOT proposed as work.

(a) RunState still carries an inline copy of DtGuard's predicate and message at Assets/Core/Run/RunState.cs:70-73, which WO-0010 excluded from migration on purpose and correctly -- reopening a dispatched order as a side effect would have been worse. The two texts are character-identical today, so WO-0010 criterion 12 holds. The latent risk is that nothing detects divergence: if anyone edits DtGuard's message, RunState silently disagrees, criterion 12 becomes false, and no test goes red, because no test anywhere asserts the message text of WaveScheduler's or PlayerMotor's exception at all -- the only message assertions in the suite are Criterion12_ExceptionMessageAccuratelyStatesPredidate at Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/WO0008CriteriaVerificationTests.cs:568, and they check RunState only, via Contains.Substring rather than equality. I am not proposing an engineering work order for this, for two reasons: migrating RunState is a two-line change better carried by whatever order next touches that file, and the divergence risk is not engineering's to close, it is mine. The correct instrument is a test in Assets/Tests/Core.Tests asserting that RunState.Tick, WaveScheduler.Tick and PlayerMotor.Tick all throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException with the identical Message for the identical non-finite input. That pins criterion 12 mechanically, needs no production change, sits inside quality's own write scope, and would go red the moment the copies diverge. It is directed as quality work in RUL-0002 rather than proposed here.

(b) WaveScheduler.Tick appends O(dt / _interval) items to the caller's buffer in a single call for any large finite dt, so even in the region where the loop does terminate, a dt of 1e6 seconds at _interval 2f appends five hundred thousand SpawnRequests. That is an unbounded allocation, which WO-0010's goal sentence names as a thing to prevent, but no criterion of WO-0010 states a bound and the class comment at WaveScheduler.cs:7-13 documents carrying the remainder across ticks as deliberate behaviour. Capping the per-call spawn count would be a design decision about what a 5-second hitch should produce, which is the game designer's call and not a defect for engineering to fix unasked. Logged here so it is not re-derived next round. It becomes work only if someone decides the catch-up behaviour needs a ceiling; it is distinct from CHA-0001, which is about non-termination and is a defect.
